title: Protocol to measure the membrane tension and bending modulus of cells using optical tweezers and scanning electron microscopy
protocol: Turn on all electronic components for the optical tweezers system including power supply, microscope, positioning stage, computer, temperature control, atmosphere control.
Activate anti-vibration table.
Ensure all required software is loaded correctly.
Start and calibrate any additional gadgets like joystick used for controlling stage position.
Install or check the appropriate objective lens with a numerical aperture (NA) between 1.2 and 1.4 for tether extraction experiments.
Wait for temperature stabilization inside the chamber before introducing the sample, ensuring strict control of temperature and optimal culture conditions.
Disperse polystyrene beads within the culture medium before tether extraction.
Place the glass-bottom dish containing the dispersed beads into the microscope.
Apply an appropriate immersion oil immediately before sample positioning.
Position the glass-bottom dish inside an atmosphere-controlled acrylic chamber.
Approach the objective lens to the glass-bottom dish until the immersion oil touches the coverslip.
Adjust CO2 level to 5% after proper placement of the sample.
Wait for CO2 stabilization.
Employ Kohler Illumination procedure once atmosphere and temperature control are stabilized.
Set the laser output to approximately 1 W at the back focal plane of the objective lens.
Place a powermeter above the microscope stage to measure the laser power before and after tether pulling experiments.
Define video capture parameters in the acquisition software, setting the frame rate to at least 10 fps.
Set the total acquisition time to a minimum of 20 seconds.
Find a region of the sample clean of debris and cells.
Turn on the laser in the chosen power intensity and trap a bead with the OT.
Start the video capture, at the established parameters.
Save the video and tag it accordingly.
Approach a cell of interest in the sample.
Search for a cell with enough space around it to allow tether extraction.
Trap a nearby bead and place it near the chosen cell.
Press the OT-trapped bead against the cell membrane for 5–10 seconds.
Place the OT-trapped bead above a chosen cell.
Move the focus toward the coverslip using the microscope.
Move the OT-trapped bead toward the coverslip until it touches the cell surface.
Identify a visual change in the OT-trapped bead image caused by displacement in the optical axis direction.
Use uncoated polystyrene beads for pressing against the cell surface.
Press the OT-trapped bead against the cell surface as fast as possible to avoid cytoskeleton distortion and phagocytosis.
Move the entire sample in the xy direction to separate the bead from the cell.
Perform this step with a controlled velocity of 1.0 μm/s.
Extend the tether until a distance of 3–5 bead diameters is reached.
Maintain the extended tether for the duration of video acquisition.
Turn off the laser emission after video completion.
Observe the bead recoil following laser turn-off.
Remove the microscope condenser unit and the objective lens for laser power measurement.
Use a powermeter to verify the value of laser power P that reaches the sample.
Perform at least two different measurements of power before and after the tether pulling experiment.
Evaluate the transmittance of the lens during calibration.
Establishing the probe’s position using an image analysis software.
Open the video file in ImageJ.
Select “Image” tab, then choose “Adjust” and click on “Threshold.”
Keep the options “Default” and “B&W” selected.
Drag the lower slider to 255.
Adjust the upper slider until the bead is in optimal contrast compared to the background.
Note the threshold parameters.
Process the movie using the threshold function.
Outline a region around the trapped bead with about one diameter from each side of the bead.
Choose “Analyze particles” in the “Analyze” tab.
Determine a minimum size range of 50–100 pixels in the “Size” section.
Select “Outlines” in the “Show” section to produce outline images of identified particles.
Select “Exclude on edges” to remove frames where the particle touches or crosses boundaries.
Select “Display results” to show a table with XY position for each frame.
Process all frames with selected options.
Examine produced images of outlines for any incorrectly computed particle positions.
Save the resulting table accordingly.
Open the XY coordinates video file for the sample in KaleidaGraph.
Select “Tab” under “Delimiter.”
Choose “=1” for “Number.”
Select “Read Titles.”
Click “OK” to open the table.
Identify three columns: video frame number, X positions, and Y positions.
Select the X column by clicking its title.
Click “Summary Statistics.”
Retrieve the mean position from the generated list for the X column.
Repeat the same process for the Y column.
Alternatively, run the command “mean(c#)” in the Formula Entry window to determine the mean value of a column of # number.
Obtain both mean values for X and Y positions.
Create a new column in each table to represent the conversion of number of frames into time in seconds.
Create another new column in each table to represent the variation in the equilibrium position of the bead relative to the reference position (Δx).
Calculate Δx using XM and YM from the table, XMref and YMref as mean values for the reference position, and ψ as the pixel/micrometer ratio.
Add a sixth column in each table to represent force F in pN.
Calculate F using the equation F = βΔxP, where β is the OT spring constant per unit of power, P is the laser power measured for the experiment, and Δx is the variation calculated previously.
Run the sequence of calculations if using KaleidaGraph.
Open position data tables of experimental measures in KaleidaGraph.
Follow the described order to run the sequence of equations.
Plot the time progression of the observed force using KaleidaGraph or another software.
Select a plot profile in the “Gallery” tab for KaleidaGraph.
Choose the style as “Line,” located under “Linear.”
In the pop-up window, select the X axis with the time column (c3).
Select the Y axis as the force column (c5).
Create a plot of the force (pN) versus time (s).
Adapt another software to create a plot of the force (6th column) as a function of time (4th column) for each data table.
Note: This is an important step for quality control.
Eliminate the data if no plateau is recognized in the tether force curve.
Prepare the fixing solution by mixing 2.5% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M cacodylate buffer (pH 7.4).
Estimate the volume of the final fixing solution to be 2 mL per sample dish.
Immediately after tether extraction with optical tweezers, attach the bead used for extraction to the sample coverslip by pressing it against the coverslip for 5-10 seconds.
Repeat the procedure to extract several tethers from the same cell and other surrounding cells.
Remove almost all the culture medium from the glass-bottom dish using an automatic micropipette.
Add 2 mL of fixing solution to the sample gently and from the side of the dish.
Incubate the sample in the fixing solution for 15 minutes under the microscope.
Carefully remove the sample from the microscope after the initial incubation.
Gently remove the fixing solution from the side of the dish.
Prepare a post-fixing solution containing 0.2 M sucrose, 2 mM MgCl2 in 0.1 M cacodylate buffer (pH 7.4).
Add 2 mL of the post-fixing solution to the sample gently and from the side of the dish.
Store the samples at 4°C if pausing the procedure for later continuation.
Wait for at least 40 min after post-fixing the samples.
Change the post-fixing solution very slowly and from the sides of the dishes.
Prepare five solutions of ethanol: 30%, 50%, 70%, 90%, and 100%.
Replace the post-fixing solution with 30% ethanol and incubate for 10 min at 20°C–25°C.
Rinse with the same solution and leave for another 5 min.
Repeat the steps, increasing the concentrations of ethanol until 100% is achieved.
Add coverslips to a critical-point dryer following the manufacturer’s procedures.
Wait until the entire process is complete (1 h and 30 min).
Mount the specimen stub.
Remove the dried coverslips from the critical-point dryer.
Attach the coverslips to specimen stubs using an electrically conductive carbon adhesive tape.
Coat the specimens with metallic sputtering for 45 minutes following the manufacturer’s procedures.
Place the sample into a scanning electron microscope and adjust the parameters.
Find the square on the coverslip where the chosen cell is located at lower magnification mode.
Increase the magnification to locate and image individual tethers of interest.
Open each tether scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image in ImageJ software.
Rotate the image so that the tether is vertically aligned.
Use the rectangle selection tool to draw around the tether.
Select “Analyze” and choose “Plot Profile.”
Click on the bottom option “List” and save the opened table.
Export saved tables individually into KaleidaGraph software.
Create a new scatter plot of the listed results in KaleidaGraph.
Repeat the above-described procedures for all other tether plot profiles.
Determine the mean tether radius value for each specific experimental condition.
Export saved tables individually if using different software.
Open and analyze exported tables on the specified software.
Create a new plot of the listed results.
Perform curve fitting using the given equation where Bi > 0, i = 0, 1, 2, yL, yR, and ξ are parameters to be determined.
Retrieve the values of yL and yR from the fitted curve.
Convert the tether diameter (difference between yL and yR) to micrometers or nanometers based on the pixel scale if necessary.
Calculate the mean tether radius as half the difference between yL and yR.
